title: GPS Position Modes, Loiter & Return-to-Home
html:
What GPS buys you

The flight controller fuses the GPS receiver, barometer, magnetometer (compass) and the IMU in an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate an absolute position. Once that estimate is trustworthy, the autopilot can hold a spot in 3D space instead of just leveling the craft. This is the foundation of every autonomous behavior in this part.

The position-aware flight modes

Mode (ArduPilot / PX4)What it doesNeeds GPS?
Stabilize / ManualSelf-levels (ArduPilot) or rate (PX4); no position holdNo
AltHold / AltitudeHolds altitude on baro; you fly positionNo
Loiter / PositionHolds 3D position; stick input nudges itYes
PosHoldLike Loiter but more direct stick feelYes
Auto / MissionFlies a stored waypoint missionYes
RTL / ReturnClimbs to set altitude, flies home, landsYes

How the home point is set

ArduPilot sets home automatically when the vehicle first arms with a good 3D GPS fix. That single moment matters: home is latched at the launch point, and RTL/Return-to-Home (RTH) flies back to those exact coordinates. PX4 behaves similarly. If you arm before the GPS has settled, home can be latched tens of metres off — and RTH will fly the craft to the wrong place, possibly into a tree or over a road.

What 'good lock' actually means

  • Satellites: 6 is a bare minimum; aim for 10+ before arming for any autonomous flight.
  • HDOP (horizontal dilution of precision): below 1.5 is good; 2.0+ means a sloppy fix.
  • EKF / position variance: Mission Planner shows an EKF status bar; PX4/QGC shows a position estimate health flag. Both must be green.
  • Compass health: a bad compass calibration makes Loiter 'toilet-bowl' (orbit in a widening circle). Calibrate away from metal, rebar and cars.

RTH altitude — the number that saves the aircraft

ArduPilot's RTL_ALT (in cm, e.g. 3000 = 30 m) is the altitude the craft climbs to before flying home. PX4 uses RTL_RETURN_ALT. Set it above the tallest obstacle between you and home. The autopilot does not see obstacles in basic RTH — it flies a straight line at the set altitude, so a 30 m tree line with a 20 m RTH altitude is a crash.

SAFETY.
Never trust RTH you have not verified. Confirm home is set at your feet (check the GCS map marker), confirm RTH altitude clears all obstacles, and know that RTH at poor GPS lock can fly to a phantom home dozens of metres away.
Toilet-bowling.
If Loiter spirals outward, it is almost always a compass problem (declination, calibration, or interference from current-carrying wires near the compass). Land immediately in a non-GPS mode.

Failsafe RTH

RTH is also the usual failsafe action on RC loss or low battery. Configure the battery failsafe voltage with margin to actually make it home — a craft at the field edge needs reserve to climb to RTH altitude and traverse back.

▸Hands-On

Write a pre-flight RTH safety checklist and reason about a bad-lock home.

  1. List preconditions: 10+ sats, HDOP < 1.5, EKF/position green, compass calibrated, home marker visible on GCS at launch point.
  2. Set RTH altitude above the tallest obstacle on your field; write the number down.
  3. Describe what happens if home latches with HDOP 4.0: home is offset, RTH flies to the wrong coordinate, and the descent may occur over an obstacle or hazard. Write the recovery action (switch to Loiter/PosHold or Stabilize and fly manually).

title: Ground Stations: Mission Planner & QGroundControl
html:
Two ground stations, one job

A Ground Control Station (GCS) is the laptop/tablet app that talks to your autopilot over MAVLink: it shows telemetry, lets you plan missions, tune parameters and arm/command the vehicle. The two dominant open-source GCS apps map roughly to the two firmware families.

Mission PlannerQGroundControl
Primary firmwareArduPilot (also PX4)PX4 (also ArduPilot)
PlatformWindows (Mono on Mac/Linux)Win / Mac / Linux / Android / iOS
StrengthsDeep parameter access, log analysis, scriptingClean UI, survey planning, cross-platform

Installing

  • Mission Planner: download the installer from ardupilot.org; it bundles the .NET runtime and drivers. First launch installs the SiK radio / USB drivers.
  • QGroundControl: download from qgroundcontrol.com. On Linux, chmod +x QGroundControl.AppImage and add your user to the dialout group so USB serial works.

Connecting to a vehicle

Connection is by transport + baud:

  • USB: pick the COM/tty port; ArduPilot USB is typically 115200 baud.
  • Telemetry radio (SiK 433/915 MHz): usually 57600 baud.
  • UDP/TCP: used for SITL and companion-computer links.

In Mission Planner, the connect dropdown is top-right; choose the port, set baud, click Connect. In QGC, connections are auto-detected or added under Application Settings > Comm Links.

Connecting to SITL (no hardware)

SITL (Software In The Loop) runs the real firmware on your PC and outputs MAVLink over UDP. ArduPilot SITL defaults to broadcasting on udp:127.0.0.1:14550.

connect QGC/MP to SITL
# ArduPilot SITL spits MAVLink to UDP 14550 by default Mission Planner: top-right dropdown > UDP > port 14550 > Connect QGroundControl: Application Settings > Comm Links > Add Type: UDP Port: 14550 > Connect # once connected you'll see the HUD horizon move and the map center on the home location

Reading the HUD

The Heads-Up Display shows artificial horizon, airspeed/groundspeed, altitude, heading, battery and GPS/EKF status. The map shows the vehicle icon, home (the 'H' marker), and any loaded mission. Get fluent here before you ever fly autonomously — the HUD is how you catch a bad attitude estimate or a wandering position.

Two GCS, same protocol.
Because both speak MAVLink, you can connect QGC to ArduPilot or Mission Planner to PX4. Use whichever you prefer for a given task — many pros plan surveys in QGC but analyze logs in Mission Planner.
SAFETY.
When connected to a real vehicle, props can spin the instant you arm. Practice all arming/commands in SITL first, and keep props off the bench until you are deliberately doing a motor test.
▸Hands-On

Get a live GCS-to-SITL connection up.

  1. Install Mission Planner or QGroundControl.
  2. Start ArduPilot SITL (next lessons cover the command) so it outputs to UDP 14550.
  3. Add a UDP comm link on port 14550 and connect.
  4. Confirm the HUD horizon responds and the map centers on home; screenshot the live connection showing map + HUD.

title: Waypoint Missions, Surveys & Geofences
html:
Anatomy of a waypoint mission

A mission is an ordered list of commands stored on the autopilot. Most are waypoints (MAV_CMD_NAV_WAYPOINT) carrying latitude, longitude and altitude, but the list can also include takeoff, loiter, change-speed, do-set-servo (trigger a camera) and land/RTL commands. In Auto/Mission mode the autopilot executes them in sequence.

Building a mission in a GCS

  • Mission Planner: the Plan tab. Click on the map to drop waypoints; each row gets a command type, altitude and acceptance radius. The first item is often TAKEOFF; end with RTL or LAND.
  • QGroundControl: the Plan view. Add waypoints, then upload with the Upload button. QGC has dedicated Survey and Corridor Scan patterns.

Altitude reference — the classic gotcha

Waypoint altitude is usually relative to home (the launch point), not above sea level and not above the terrain under the waypoint. If your field slopes up 20 m toward a waypoint, a 30 m relative altitude leaves only 10 m of clearance there. ArduPilot and QGC both support terrain following (using SRTM terrain data) to hold altitude above ground instead — enable it deliberately when flying over varying terrain.

Surveys (the lawnmower pattern)

A survey tool takes a polygon you draw over an area and auto-generates parallel sweep lines ("lawnmower") plus camera trigger points. You specify the camera, desired Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) or altitude, and front/side overlap (typically 75% front / 65% side for photogrammetry). The tool computes line spacing and shot interval. We design grids in detail in Lesson 7.9.

Geofences: containment, not a suggestion

A geofence is a boundary the autopilot enforces itself. ArduPilot supports:

Fence typeParameter / shapePurpose
Altitude (max)FENCE_ALT_MAXCeiling
CircleFENCE_RADIUS around homeKeep within radius
Polygon (inclusion)drawn in GCSStay inside the shape
Polygon (exclusion)drawn in GCSKeep out of a zone

Enable with FENCE_ENABLE = 1 and pick the breach action via FENCE_ACTION (e.g. RTL or Land). On a breach the autopilot takes over regardless of pilot intent. QGC has a similar GeoFence editor in the Plan view.

SAFETY.
Treat altitude and geofence limits as your hard containment, especially when testing autonomous code. Set a modest FENCE_RADIUS and FENCE_ALT_MAX at a clear field so a buggy script cannot fly the craft into a road, crowd or airspace boundary. Verify the breach action does something safe at your specific site.

Airspace.
A geofence does not authorize flight. You are still responsible for staying within legal altitude limits (e.g. 400 ft AGL in many jurisdictions under standard rules) and out of restricted airspace. Verify current FAA/local rules and any authorizations before flying.
▸Hands-On

Plan and fly a contained waypoint mission in SITL.

  1. In your GCS Plan view, drop a TAKEOFF to 15 m, four waypoints in a box at 30 m, then RTL.
  2. Add a circular geofence (e.g. 200 m radius) and a max altitude (e.g. 50 m); set the breach action to RTL.
  3. Upload the mission to SITL, switch to Auto, and arm.
  4. Watch it fly and log the flight path; confirm it stayed inside the fence.

title: The MAVLink Protocol Explained
html:
What MAVLink is

MAVLink (Micro Air Vehicle Link) is the lightweight binary messaging protocol that nearly every modern autopilot, GCS and companion computer uses to talk. It is designed for low-bandwidth, lossy links (a 57600-baud radio) and serializes structured messages into compact byte frames. Everything in this part — GCS telemetry, Python scripts, computer-vision guidance — rides on MAVLink.

The frame

A MAVLink v2 frame is a start byte (0xFD), payload length, sequence number, system ID, component ID, message ID, the payload, and a CRC. System ID identifies the vehicle (autopilot is usually ID 1); component ID distinguishes parts (autopilot, gimbal, companion computer). Your script picks its own sysid/compid so the vehicle knows who is talking.

Messages vs commands

  • Messages stream state, e.g. HEARTBEAT, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, ATTITUDE. The autopilot pushes these continuously.
  • Commands are requests you send, often via COMMAND_LONG/COMMAND_INT with a MAV_CMD_* id (e.g. MAV_CMD_NAV_TAKEOFF, MAV_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM). The vehicle replies with COMMAND_ACK telling you accepted/denied.

The heartbeat — the protocol's pulse

Every node sends a HEARTBEAT at ~1 Hz. It carries the vehicle type, autopilot type, base/custom mode, and a system status. A GCS uses heartbeats to detect link loss; if no heartbeat arrives for a timeout, it declares the vehicle lost. Your own script should also emit a heartbeat so the vehicle does not treat it as a dead GCS and trigger a failsafe.

three common MAVLink messages
HEARTBEAT ~1 Hz: vehicle type, autopilot, armed flag, flight mode GLOBAL_POSITION_INT lat/lon (1e7 deg), alt & relative_alt (mm), velocity vx/vy/vz ATTITUDE roll/pitch/yaw (rad) + angular rates, from the EKF SYS_STATUS battery voltage/current, sensor health bitmask STATUSTEXT human-readable warnings/errors from the autopilot

Telemetry rates & the message interval

You do not get every message at full rate by default. You request streams: legacy REQUEST_DATA_STREAM or the modern MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL (specify message id + interval in microseconds). Asking for high rates on a slow radio saturates the link and drops packets — request only what you need.

How tools speak it

You rarely hand-assemble frames. pymavlink generates Python bindings from the message XML definitions. MAVSDK and DroneKit wrap MAVLink in higher-level APIs. Mission Planner and QGC both have a live MAVLink Inspector showing every message and field at its current rate.

Units gotcha.
MAVLink packs to integers to save bytes: lat/lon are degrees x 1e7, altitudes in mm, angles in radians. Convert in your code or you will fly to the wrong continent.
▸Hands-On

Inspect live MAVLink from SITL and document three messages.

  1. Connect Mission Planner (Ctrl+F > MAVLink Inspector) or QGC's MAVLink Inspector to SITL.
  2. Find HEARTBEAT, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT and ATTITUDE.
  3. For each, write down its rate and what its key fields carry (e.g. GLOBAL_POSITION_INT: lat/lon x1e7, relative_alt in mm).

title: Setting Up SITL & a Python Control Environment
html:
Why SITL first, always

SITL runs the genuine ArduPilot or PX4 firmware as a desktop process with a simulated physics model. Your scripts, missions and bugs behave exactly as they would on hardware — except a crash costs nothing. Every line of autonomy code in this part is developed and proven in SITL before it ever touches a real aircraft.

Installing ArduPilot SITL

ArduPilot SITL via sim_vehicle.py
# one-time: clone and set up the toolchain git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/ArduPilot/ardupilot cd ardupilot Tools/environment_install/install-prereqs-ubuntu.sh -y # or the mac script . ~/.profile # launch a simulated copter; --map shows a map, --console a status window sim_vehicle.py -v ArduCopter --map --console # SITL now serves MAVLink on udp:127.0.0.1:14550 (and 14551)

PX4 alternative: make px4_sitl gazebo (or jMAVSim) from the PX4-Autopilot tree; it outputs MAVLink on UDP 14540 (offboard) / 14550 (GCS).

Three Python libraries — pick by job

LibraryLevelBest for
pymavlinkLow (raw messages)Full control, custom messages, learning the protocol
DroneKitHigh (object model)Quick ArduPilot scripts (note: less maintained)
MAVSDKHigh (async, PX4-first)Modern PX4 apps, async/await Python

Setting up the Python environment

venv + libraries
python3 -m venv droneenv source droneenv/bin/activate pip install pymavlink mavsdk dronekit # pymavlink needs the future package on some systems; pip handles it

First connection — print heartbeat & mode

connect.py (pymavlink)
from pymavlink import mavutil # match the SITL output endpoint m = mavutil.mavlink_connection('udp:127.0.0.1:14550') m.wait_heartbeat() # blocks until first HEARTBEAT print('heartbeat from sys %d comp %d' % (m.target_system, m.target_component)) # decode the flight mode from the heartbeat print('mode:', m.flightmode)
Sharing one stream.
SITL only fans out so many UDP endpoints. Run MAVProxy (it ships with sim_vehicle.py) as a hub and use output add 127.0.0.1:14551 to feed your script while a GCS stays on 14550. Otherwise you fight over the port.
SAFETY.
Keep the exact connection string different for sim vs hardware, and put a loud comment at the top of every script stating whether it targets SITL or a real vehicle. The number-one cause of unintended real-world flights is running a sim script against a live, propped drone.
▸Hands-On

Stand up SITL and confirm a Python link.

  1. Launch ArduCopter SITL with sim_vehicle.py -v ArduCopter --map --console.
  2. Create a venv and pip install pymavlink.
  3. Run the connect.py script above; confirm it prints the heartbeat sys/comp IDs and the current flight mode (e.g. STABILIZE).

title: Scripting Flight: Arm, Takeoff & Goto in Python
html:
The autonomous flight sequence

Every mission script follows the same skeleton: connect, wait for the vehicle to be armable, set a mode that accepts commands (GUIDED), arm, take off, navigate, then land or RTL. We will use pymavlink because it shows exactly what is on the wire; DroneKit/MAVSDK wrap these same steps.

Why GUIDED mode

In ArduPilot, GUIDED mode lets an external program send position/velocity setpoints in real time — it is the mode for scripted and companion-computer control. (PX4's equivalent is Offboard mode, which additionally requires a continuous setpoint stream or it drops out.) You cannot just send a goto in Loiter; the vehicle must be in GUIDED/Offboard.

fly.py (pymavlink, ArduCopter SITL)
from pymavlink import mavutil import time m = mavutil.mavlink_connection('udp:127.0.0.1:14550') m.wait_heartbeat() # 1) set GUIDED mode mode_id = m.mode_mapping()['GUIDED'] m.set_mode(mode_id) # 2) arm (param1=1 to arm) m.mav.command_long_send(m.target_system, m.target_component, mavutil.mavlink.MAV_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM, 0, 1,0,0,0,0,0,0) m.motors_armed_wait() print('armed') # 3) takeoff to 10 m (last param = altitude) m.mav.command_long_send(m.target_system, m.target_component, mavutil.mavlink.MAV_CMD_NAV_TAKEOFF, 0, 0,0,0,0,0,0, 10) time.sleep(10) # wait for climb (better: poll relative_alt) # 4) goto a lat/lon at 10 m using SET_POSITION_TARGET_GLOBAL_INT m.mav.set_position_target_global_int_send( 0, m.target_system, m.target_component, mavutil.mavlink.MAV_FRAME_GLOBAL_RELATIVE_ALT_INT, 0b110111111000, # type_mask: use position only int(-35.3621 * 1e7), int(149.1655 * 1e7), 10, # lat,lon (x1e7), alt(m) 0,0,0, 0,0,0, 0,0) time.sleep(20) # 5) land where it is m.set_mode(m.mode_mapping()['LAND']) print('landing')

Key details that bite beginners

  • Arm checks: SITL enforces pre-arm checks (GPS, EKF). If arming is rejected, read the STATUSTEXT message — it tells you why.
  • Takeoff only works in GUIDED and only after arming. Set mode, then arm, then takeoff, in that order.
  • Don't sleep blindly. Replace fixed time.sleep with polling: read GLOBAL_POSITION_INT.relative_alt until it reaches the target. Sleeps are fine for a first demo only.
  • type_mask in the position target selects which fields are active (position vs velocity vs acceleration). Get it wrong and the vehicle ignores your command.
SAFETY — sim only.
Run this against SITL exclusively until you fully trust it. On real hardware this code arms motors and flies the aircraft autonomously; props will spin the moment arming succeeds. Test outdoors only after bench-validating logic with props removed, at a clear field, with a geofence and a manual-override mode on your transmitter.
▸Hands-On

Fly a full arm-takeoff-goto-land script in SITL.

  1. With SITL running, run the fly.py script above (edit the lat/lon to a point near your SITL home).
  2. Watch the map: confirm it arms, climbs to 10 m, flies to the waypoint, and lands.
  3. Improve it: replace the takeoff sleep with a loop that reads relative_alt until ≥ 9.5 m.
  4. Pull the SITL log (.bin/.tlog) and confirm the recorded path matches your commands.

title: Adding a Companion Computer: Raspberry Pi & Jetson
html:
Why add a second brain

The flight controller (FC) is a real-time microcontroller dedicated to stabilization and navigation — it has no spare cycles for computer vision, machine learning or a cellular link. A companion computer is a small Linux board mounted on the drone that runs your heavy code and talks to the FC over MAVLink. The FC keeps flying the aircraft; the companion tells it where to go.

Choosing the board

BoardStrengthUse it for
Raspberry Pi 4 / 5Cheap, huge communityTelemetry relay, basic OpenCV, MAVLink scripting
NVIDIA Jetson NanoCUDA GPU on a budgetEntry deep-learning inference
Jetson Orin Nano / NXStrong GPU, modernReal-time object detection, depth, SLAM

The physical link: companion to FC

The standard link is a serial UART from a spare FC telemetry port (e.g. TELEM2) to the companion's UART pins. Wire only TX, RX and GND — and cross them (FC TX to Pi RX, FC RX to Pi TX). Common baud is 921600 for an onboard link (far faster than a radio). Set the FC's serial protocol on that port to MAVLink2 (ArduPilot: SERIAL2_PROTOCOL = 2, SERIAL2_BAUD = 921). USB also works but a dedicated UART is more robust.

companion <-> FC link (diagram)
[GPS] [Camera CSI/USB] | | | +----------------+ | | Companion (Pi/ | | | Jetson) Linux | | | OpenCV/MAVSDK | | +----------------+ | | UART (TX/RX/GND, 921600) | | FC TX -> Pi RX, FC RX -> Pi TX +------------------+ | Flight Controller| TELEM2 = MAVLink2 | (ArduPilot/PX4) | +------------------+ | | [Motors] [RC/Telem radio] Power: 5V BEC -> Pi/Jetson (DO NOT back-power FC from companion)

Power — get this right

Companion boards are hungry: a Pi 5 wants up to 5 A at 5 V; a Jetson Orin can pull more. Feed it from a dedicated, properly rated 5 V BEC/UBEC off the main battery, not from the FC's 5 V rail. Brownouts cause silent reboots mid-flight. Use thick enough wire and a common ground with the FC.

Software stack to install

  • OS: Raspberry Pi OS Lite (headless) or NVIDIA JetPack (Ubuntu + CUDA).
  • MAVLink: pymavlink, MAVSDK, or mavlink-router to fan the FC stream to several consumers.
  • Vision: OpenCV; on Jetson, TensorRT / DeepStream for accelerated inference.
  • Comms: a 4G/5G modem or WiFi for live telemetry/video off-board.
  • Autostart: a systemd service so your code runs on boot.
Test on the bench first.
Bring up the companion-to-FC link with SITL or a propless FC and confirm you receive heartbeats over the UART before you ever bolt it to a flying airframe.
SAFETY.
A companion in GUIDED/Offboard can command full autonomous flight. Always keep a transmitter mode switch that drops the FC into a manual/Loiter mode the companion cannot override, and validate the link-loss behaviour (the companion should command a safe action if it crashes).
▸Hands-On

Design a complete companion-computer setup.

  1. Pick a board (Pi vs Jetson) for your intended workload and justify it.
  2. Draw the wiring: FC TELEM port to companion UART (TX/RX/GND crossed), the camera, and a separate 5 V BEC for power.
  3. List the FC params to set (serial protocol = MAVLink2, baud 921600).
  4. List the software you would install (OS, pymavlink/MAVSDK, OpenCV, systemd autostart, comms).

title: Computer Vision with OpenCV: Tracking & Avoidance
html:
From pixels to flight commands

Computer vision turns a camera frame into a decision the drone can act on. The pipeline is always: capture frame → detect target → compute an error → convert error to a MAVLink command → loop. OpenCV (Python cv2) handles capture and detection; pymavlink/MAVSDK handle the command. This runs on the companion computer, not the FC.

A simple color tracker

The classic starting point: track a colored object by converting to HSV (more lighting-robust than RGB), threshold for the color, find the largest contour, and take its centroid.

track.py (OpenCV color centroid)
import cv2, numpy as np cap = cv2.VideoCapture('clip.mp4') # or 0 for a live camera while True: ok, frame = cap.read() if not ok: break hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV) mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (40,70,70), (80,255,255)) # green cnts,_ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE) if cnts: c = max(cnts, key=cv2.contourArea) M = cv2.moments(c) cx, cy = int(M['m10']/M['m00']), int(M['m01']/M['m00']) h, w = frame.shape[:2] err_x = (cx - w/2) / (w/2) # -1..+1, target left/right of center err_y = (cy - h/2) / (h/2) print('err', round(err_x,2), round(err_y,2)) # err_x > 0 means target is right of center -> command a right/yaw correction

Turning error into guidance

The normalized error feeds a controller (often a simple P controller: command = gain x error). For a tracking/follow behaviour you typically map:

  • Horizontal error (err_x) → yaw rate or lateral velocity to center the target.
  • Target size / vertical error → forward velocity (move closer if the target is small/far).

You send these as a velocity setpoint with SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED (body frame), with the type_mask set to use velocities, not positions. The autopilot must be in GUIDED/Offboard.

Detection beyond color

  • ArUco / AprilTag markers (built into OpenCV) for precise relative pose — great for precision landing.
  • Optical flow for motion/velocity estimation and basic avoidance cues.
  • Deep models (YOLO via TensorRT on Jetson) for robust object detection in clutter.

Obstacle avoidance

Avoidance needs depth, not just a 2D detection: a stereo camera (e.g. Intel RealSense), a depth-from-LiDAR sensor, or a learned mono-depth model. The depth map feeds either ArduPilot's built-in OA_* (object avoidance) via OBSTACLE_DISTANCE/DISTANCE_SENSOR MAVLink messages, or your own controller that slows and steers around the nearest return.

Latency is the enemy.
The control loop must keep up. A 30 ms detection that arrives 200 ms late commands the drone toward where the target was. Profile your loop, cap resolution, and offload to the GPU before chasing accuracy.
SAFETY.
Vision can fail silently — a lost target, a false positive, a frozen camera. Build a watchdog: if detection is stale for N frames, command zero velocity / hold position and fall back to a safe mode rather than flying on a stale command. Test all of this in SITL with a video feed before flying.
▸Hands-On

Run a color tracker and map its output to MAVLink velocity.

  1. Run track.py on a video clip containing a colored object; tune the HSV range until the centroid locks on.
  2. Print normalized err_x/err_y each frame.
  3. On paper, define a P controller: vy = Kp*err_x, vz = Kp*err_y, and which type_mask fields of SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED you would enable.
  4. Add a stale-detection watchdog that would command zero velocity if the target is lost.

title: Autonomous Patterns: Mapping Grids & Follow-Me
html:
The lawnmower mapping grid

To map an area for photogrammetry you fly parallel sweeps ("lawnmower") and trigger the camera at intervals so every point on the ground appears in multiple overlapping photos. The grid geometry is driven by your camera, your altitude, and your overlap targets.

Ground Sampling Distance (GSD)

GSD is the real-world size of one pixel on the ground — your effective resolution. It scales with altitude:

grid math
GSD (cm/px) = (sensor_width_mm * altitude_m * 100) / (focal_mm * image_width_px) example: 13.2mm sensor, 8.8mm focal, 5472px wide, 80m altitude GSD = (13.2 * 80 * 100) / (8.8 * 5472) = 2.19 cm/px footprint_width_m = GSD/100 * image_width_px = 0.0219 * 5472 = ~120 m footprint_height_m = GSD/100 * image_height_px line_spacing_m = footprint_width_m * (1 - side_overlap) side overlap ~65% = 120 * 0.35 = 42 m shot_spacing_m = footprint_height_m * (1 - front_overlap) front overlap ~75%

Overlap targets

Use caseFront overlapSide overlap
Standard orthomosaic75%65%
3D models / dense vegetation80-85%70-80%

Higher overlap = more photos = more flight time and processing, but better reconstruction and fewer holes. Most GCS survey tools (QGC Survey, Mission Planner Survey Grid) take the camera, altitude/GSD and overlaps, then compute line spacing, shot interval and total shot count for you.

Flight efficiency tips

  • Orient sweep lines along the longest dimension of the polygon to minimize turns.
  • Fly into the wind on alternate legs only if speed control compensates; constant ground speed keeps shot spacing even.
  • Account for battery: total distance = (num_lines x line_length) + turns; check it fits one pack with reserve.
  • Use terrain following over hilly ground so GSD stays constant.

Follow-Me

Follow-me keeps the drone tracking a moving target. Two common approaches:

  • GPS follow: a phone/GPS beacon streams its position to the drone (ArduPilot Follow mode / GCS follow), and the drone holds an offset (distance + altitude + bearing) from that position. Simple and robust outdoors.
  • Vision follow: the companion computer detects the subject in the camera (Lesson 7.8) and sends velocity setpoints to keep it framed. Works without a beacon but fails if the subject leaves frame or is occluded.

In both, you set a follow distance and altitude, and the autopilot continuously re-issues guided setpoints. Define behaviour for target loss (hold, climb, or RTL).

Rules.
Automated patterns do not exempt you from the rules of flight. Surveys often run near or beyond visual line of sight and at altitude — verify current FAA/local requirements (BVLOS authorization, altitude caps, overflight of people) before flying any autonomous grid or follow mission.
SAFETY.
Prove every grid and follow mission in SITL first, set a geofence and a sane RTH altitude, and keep a manual-override mode ready. Follow-me near people demands extra caution: a tracking error sends the aircraft toward the very subject you are filming.
▸Hands-On

Plan and fly an autonomous survey grid in SITL.

  1. In QGC or Mission Planner, draw a polygon over a defined area.
  2. Enter your camera spec, set altitude for a target GSD (e.g. ~2 cm/px), and 75%/65% overlap.
  3. Let the tool compute line spacing and shot count; sanity-check against the grid math above.
  4. Upload to SITL, fly it in Auto, and export the planned path (.waypoints / .plan) plus the flown log.
